mainTopic: מצוות בני נח (כישוף and כלאים), then the משנה's laws of the מגדף: which Name counts, standing and tearing, and how the witnesses testify
overview: The גמרא finishes showing that a בן נח is also forbidden in כישוף, and brings רבי אלעזר, who adds כלאים to the מצוות בני נח. שמואל learns this from the words 'אֶת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ', meaning laws already given before. For a בן נח, the rule covers only animal breeding and tree grafting, and it applies everywhere. The word order of that פסוק explains why the rest of the Torah was not already given to them. Then the גמרא returns to the משנה of the מגדף: רב אחא בר יעקב teaches, in two versions, that the four-letter Name is the one that counts. The גמרא finds sources for the judges standing (from עגלון), tearing their clothes (from חזקיהו's officials), and never fully sewing the tear (from אלישע). It discusses who must tear, and it contrasts שמואל's limits (no tearing for a גוי or a כינוי) with רבי חייא's view. Finally, ריש לקיש proves that 'אף אני כמוהו' is valid testimony by Torah law, and the גמרא explains that the משנה follows רבי עקיבא on a third witness.

steps.title: Witchcraft is placed next to the animal prohibition
steps.stepSummary: Because the פסוק about a witch sits right next to the פסוק about lying with an animal, whoever is included in the animal prohibition is also included in the witchcraft prohibition.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah says 'Do not let a witch live,' and right after it says 'Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death.' So anyone who is included in the animal prohibition is also included in 'Do not let a witch live.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a proof from two פסוקים that sit side by side. It shows that the witchcraft prohibition covers the same people as the animal prohibition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The animal prohibition applies to everyone, including בני נח. Since the witchcraft פסוק is placed right next to it, the גמרא learns that witchcraft is also forbidden for everyone, not only for Jews.

keyTerms.meaning: A witch; someone who does sorcery (כישוף)
One who lies with an animal

phrases.english: "You shall not allow a witch to live,"
phrases.notes: שמות 22:17

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב: ״כׇּל שֹׁכֵב עִם בְּהֵמָה מוֹת יוּמָת״.
phrases.english: and it is written: "Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death."
phrases.notes: שמות 22:18, the very next פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁיֶּשְׁנוֹ בִּכְלַל ״כׇּל שֹׁכֵב עִם בְּהֵמָה״ –
phrases.english: Anyone who is included in "Whoever lies with an animal"
is included in "You shall not allow a witch to live."

steps.triggerLanguage: מְכַשֵּׁפָה לֹא תְחַיֶּה וּכְתִיב כׇּל שֹׁכֵב עִם בְּהֵמָה מוֹת יוּמָת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a derivation that began before this part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witchcraft is forbidden to everyone who is bound by the animal prohibition, including בני נח.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר adds mixed species
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says בני נח were also commanded about כלאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: They were also commanded about mixing species.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי אלעזר, who adds another מצוה to the list of things בני נח were commanded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list of מצוות בני נח is usually seven. רבי אלעזר says כלאים is also on the list. The next steps will ask where this comes from and what exactly it includes.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הַכִּלְאַיִם.
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar says: Also about diverse kinds.
phrases.notes: בני נח were also commanded not to mix species.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר אַף עַל הַכִּלְאַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new item in the list of מצוות בני נח.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אלעזר, בני נח are commanded about כלאים.

steps.title: What is the source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבי אלעזר learns that בני נח were commanded about כלאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for רבי אלעזר's rule. This sets up the next step, where שמואל answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on רבי אלעזר. The גמרא just wants to know which פסוק teaches it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things learned?

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק teaches that בני נח are commanded about כלאים.

steps.title: שמואל: 'My statutes' means laws already given
steps.stepSummary: שמואל reads 'Keep My statutes' as 'keep the laws I already gave you,' meaning the כלאים laws were already given to בני נח.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: The פסוק says 'Keep My statutes.' This means: the statutes I already set for you, namely 'Do not breed your animal with another kind; do not sow your field with two kinds.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the question. He shows that the פסוק of כלאים opens with words that hint these laws were already given earlier, before מתן תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word חקותי is read as 'statutes I already set for you.' Laws given before מתן תורה were given to all mankind. So כלאים was commanded to בני נח too.

keyTerms.meaning: That I already set down for you

phrases.english: Shmuel says: As the verse states:
"My statutes you shall keep"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:19

phrases.english: statutes that I have already instituted for you:
"You shall not breed your animal with a diverse kind;
you shall not sow your field with diverse kinds."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל דְּאָמַר קְרָא אֵת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word חקותי means laws already given before, so כלאים was already commanded to בני נח.

steps.title: Which kind of mixing, and where
steps.stepSummary: Comparing 'your animal' and 'your field': for a בן נח only grafting is forbidden in the field, just like only breeding is forbidden with animals, and it applies both in ארץ ישראל and outside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as with your animal it means breeding, so too with your field it means grafting. Just as with your animal it applies both in ארץ ישראל and outside ארץ ישראל, so too with your field it applies both in ארץ ישראל and outside ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the same פסוק to define exactly what כלאים means for a בן נח. It compares the field to the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animal כלאים means breeding two kinds together, so field כלאים for a בן נח means grafting, which is like breeding. Animal כלאים applies everywhere, so field כלאים for a בן נח applies everywhere too.
steps.whatToRemember: For בני נח (according to רבי אלעזר), כלאים means only animal breeding and tree grafting, and it applies all over the world.

phrases.english: Just as your animal is with regard to breeding,
so too your field is with regard to grafting.

phrases.aramaic: מָה בְּהֶמְתְּךָ בֵּין בָּאָרֶץ בֵּין בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ,
phrases.english: Just as your animal applies both in the Land and outside the Land,

phrases.aramaic: אַף שָׂדְךָ בֵּין בָּאָרֶץ בֵּין בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ.
phrases.english: so too your field applies both in the Land and outside the Land.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה בְּהֶמְתְּךָ בְּהַרְבָּעָה אַף שָׂדְךָ בְּהַרְכָּבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses שמואל's פסוק to set the details of the rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Field כלאים for בני נח is grafting only, and both kinds apply everywhere.

steps.title: Challenge: then the whole Torah would apply to them
steps.stepSummary: If חקותי means 'laws already given,' then another פסוק that says 'keep My statutes and My laws' would mean the whole Torah was already given to בני נח.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, the פסוק 'You shall keep My statutes and My laws' would also mean: statutes I already set for you?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל's reading of the word חקותי. It points to another פסוק with the same word that cannot mean this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same word חקותי appears in a פסוק about all the מצוות. If it always means 'already given,' then all the מצוות would have been given before, which cannot be right. So שמואל's reading seems to prove too much.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (then this strange result follows)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the whole Torah applies to בני נח. It is showing that שמואל's reading would lead to that impossible result, so his reading needs defending.

phrases.english: If that is so:
"You shall keep My statutes and My ordinances"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 18:5

phrases.english: would that also mean statutes that I have already instituted for you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's reading from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's reading of חקותי as 'laws already given'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same word appears in a פסוק about all the מצוות. Reading it the same way would mean the whole Torah was already given to בני נח, which is impossible.

steps.title: Word order shows which statutes were given earlier
steps.stepSummary: The other פסוק says 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת חֻקֹּתַי,' which means the laws given now. The כלאים פסוק says 'אֶת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ,' which means laws that were already given from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the פסוק says 'And you shall keep My statutes,' which means the statutes I am giving you now. Here, it says 'My statutes you shall keep,' which means: the statutes you already had from the beginning, keep them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 6 by pointing to the different word order in the two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 argued that if חֻקֹּתַי means 'old laws,' the whole תורה would have been given to בני נח. The answer is that the meaning depends on how the פסוק is built. When 'My statutes' comes first, the stress is on statutes that already existed. When 'you shall keep' comes first, it means the laws being given now. So only כלאים is treated as an older law that בני נח already had.

keyTerms.meaning: Of now, given at this time

steps.whatToRemember: The rule that בני נח were commanded about כלאים rests on the word order 'אֶת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ.' Putting 'My statutes' first points to laws that were already given.

phrases.english: There — "And you shall keep My statutes" — means of now.
phrases.notes: ויקרא 18:5. In this פסוק 'you shall keep' comes first, so it's about the laws being given right now.

phrases.english: Here — "My statutes you shall keep" —
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:19, the כלאים פסוק. Here 'My statutes' comes first.

phrases.english: means: statutes from the beginning, you shall keep.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual distinction: the two פסוקים have different word order.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word חֻקֹּתַי in any פסוק means laws that were already given, so the whole תורה would apply to בני נח.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the order 'אֶת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ' means earlier laws, so only כלאים was given to בני נח before.

steps.title: A blasphemer is liable only for cursing the four-letter Name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the משנה of רבי יהושע בן קרחה. רב אחא בר יעקב rules that a blasphemer is liable only for cursing the four-letter Name, not the two-letter Name.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: רבי יהושע בן קרחה said, etc. רב אחא בר יעקב said: He is not liable unless he curses the four-letter Name. This leaves out the two-letter Name, for which he is not liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the topic of בני נח and returns to the משנה about the blasphemer (מגדף). רב אחא בר יעקב gives a rule about which Name of ה׳ counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new point is the exact limit of the punishment. It applies only to the four-letter Name. Cursing the two-letter Name does not bring that punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc.; the rest of the quote continues
That he 'blesses'; a polite way of saying 'curses'

steps.confusionAlert: 'Bless' here really means 'curse.' The גמרא uses the opposite word on purpose so it does not have to say something so terrible.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה about the blasphemer. The 'etc.' covers his words about saying 'יוסי' in place of the Name.

phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
He is not liable unless he "blesses"
the four-letter Name,
which leaves out the two-letter Name, for which he is not liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיְּבָרֵךְ שֵׁם בֶּן אַרְבַּע אוֹתִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the בני נח discussion and returns to the משנה's laws about the blasphemer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blasphemer is liable only for cursing the four-letter Name, not the two-letter Name.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious from the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב אחא needed to say this. The משנה already uses 'יוסי,' a four-letter word, in place of the Name.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious! We learned in the משנה: 'Let יוסי strike יוסי.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אחא, saying his rule seems to add nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In court, the משנה has the witnesses say 'יוסי' instead of the Name. יוסי has four letters, which seems to show that the four-letter Name is the one that counts. So רב אחא's statement looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Let יוסי strike יוסי: the stand-in phrase used in court

phrases.english: That's obvious!
We learned: "Let Yosei strike Yosei"!
phrases.notes: In Hebrew, יוסי has four letters, just like the four-letter Name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אחא's ruling in Step 8 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's four-letter stand-in already shows that the four-letter Name is needed, so his statement teaches nothing new.

steps.title: The משנה's wording might have been just an example
steps.stepSummary: Without רב אחא, we might think the משנה picked 'יוסי' only as a casual example. He teaches that only the four-letter Name makes a person liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that the משנה just used a random phrase as an example. So רב אחא teaches us that it really must be the four-letter Name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by explaining what mistake רב אחא's statement prevents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading only the משנה, we could think 'יוסי' was a handy name chosen by chance, with no message about the number of letters. רב אחא makes clear that the four letters really matter. Cursing a shorter Name does not make one liable for this punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: Just a random example, nothing exact

steps.whatToRemember: Liability for a blasphemer requires cursing the four-letter Name. The משנה's 'יוסי' was chosen on purpose, not as a random example.

phrases.english: You might have said:
it just used a random phrase as an example,
so he teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: מִילְּתָא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא דְּנָקֵט, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: the statement prevents a possible misreading of the משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's 'יוסי' was just a casual example and teaches nothing about how many letters are needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only cursing the four-letter Name makes a person liable.

steps.title: A second version: the four-letter Name also counts
steps.stepSummary: In another version, רב אחא בר יעקב learns from the משנה that cursing the four-letter Name is enough to make one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רב אחא בר יעקב said: Learn from the משנה that the four-letter Name is also a Name for which one is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way that people reported רב אחא בר יעקב's teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, רב אחא said the four-letter Name counts but a two-letter Name does not. In this version, his point runs the other way: you do not need a longer, greater Name. The four-letter Name already counts.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (a second version of a teaching)

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions agree that the four-letter Name counts. They differ only on what he was ruling out: a smaller Name (first version) or the need for a bigger Name (second version).

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
Learn from it (the משנה):
the four-letter Name
is also a Name (for which one is liable).

steps.triggerLanguage: איכא דאמרי: אמר רב אחא בר יעקב, שמע מינה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of the teaching from step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cursing with the four-letter Name is enough for liability; a greater Name is not required.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious from the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב אחא needed to say this, since the משנה already uses the four-letter 'יוסי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious! We learned in the משנה: 'Let יוסי strike יוסי.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges this second version, asking why it needed to be said at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה replaces God's Name with 'יוסי', which has four letters. That already seems to show that a four-letter Name is enough. So רב אחא seems to be teaching nothing new.

phrases.english: That is obvious!
We learned (in the משנה): 'Let Yosi strike Yosi'!
phrases.notes: 'יוסי' stands in for God's Name in court, and it has four letters, just like the Name.

steps.triggerLanguage: פשיטא! יכה יוסי את יוסי תנן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the statement in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for רב אחא's statement in its second version
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's use of a four-letter stand-in already shows the four-letter Name is enough, so the statement adds nothing.

steps.title: We might have thought a greater Name is needed
steps.stepSummary: Without רב אחא, we might think liability needs a greater Name and that 'יוסי' was just a casual example.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: one is not liable unless there is a great Name, and the משנה just picked a random word. So רב אחא teaches us that the four-letter Name is enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing the mistake we could have made without רב אחא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might have read 'יוסי' as just a sample word, not as a hint about the number of letters. Then we could think only a longer, greater Name makes one liable. רב אחא teaches that the four-letter detail is exact.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (the mistaken first idea)
A great Name, a longer Name of God
Just a random word or example

steps.whatToRemember: In this version, רב אחא teaches that cursing the four-letter Name is enough; you do not need a longer, greater Name.

phrases.english: You might have said:
(one is not liable) unless there is a great Name,
phrases.notes: A 'great Name' means one of the longer Names of God, with many more letters.

phrases.english: and (the משנה) just picked a random word,
so he teaches us (that the four-letter Name is enough).

steps.triggerLanguage: מהו דתימא: עד דאיכא שם רבה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows a reasonable mistake that the statement prevents
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'יוסי' was a random example, and only a greater Name makes one liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: The four-letter detail in 'יוסי' is exact; the four-letter Name makes one liable.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: when the judgment is finished
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה about what happens when the judgment is finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'When the judgment is finished,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next topic by quoting the משנה's words. The משנה says that at the end, the oldest witness repeats the curse exactly, and the judges stand and tear their clothes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא only quotes the opening words and writes 'etc.' The part it is about to ask about is that the judges stand up.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc., and so on (the rest of the quote)

phrases.english: 'When the judgment is finished,' etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves רב אחא's teaching and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: At the end of the trial the curse is repeated, and the judges stand and tear their clothing.

steps.title: Where do we learn that the judges stand?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that the judges must stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: That they stand: how do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for the משנה's rule that the judges stand up when they hear the curse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Standing is a sign of honor. The גמרא wants a פסוק to show that honor must be shown when God's Name is heard.

keyTerms.meaning: How do we know this? What is the source?

phrases.english: That they stand: how do we know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of a detail in the משנה quoted in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source for the rule that the judges stand when hearing God's Name in the curse.

steps.title: עגלון stood up when אהוד mentioned God
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק בר אמי brings the פסוק where עגלון, king of מואב, got up from his chair at the mention of God.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק בר אמי said: The פסוק says, 'And אהוד came to him while he was sitting in his cool upper room, which he had to himself alone. And אהוד said: I have a message from God for you. And he got up from his chair.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק בר אמי answers the question with a פסוק from שופטים about עגלון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When אהוד said he had a message from God, עגלון stood up from his chair. That shows that hearing God mentioned calls for standing. The next step explains how this teaches the judges' rule.

keyTerms.meaning: עגלון, the king of מואב who ruled over ישראל
אהוד, the judge who came to עגלון with a 'message from God'

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami said:
As the verse says,
phrases.notes: שופטים 3:20

phrases.english: 'And Ehud came to him,
while he was sitting in the cool upper room
that was his alone.
And Ehud said:
I have a message from God for you.
And he got up from his chair.'
phrases.notes: 'He' is עגלון, who stood up when God was mentioned.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רבי יצחק בר אמי: דאמר קרא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15 with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is עגלון standing up when אהוד mentioned God (שופטים 3:20).

steps.title: If a gentile king stood, surely a Jew must stand
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק teaches through a קל וחומר: עגלון stood for a mere title of God, so a Jew hearing the שם המפורש surely must stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this a קל וחומר? If עגלון, king of מואב, a gentile who knew God only by a title, stood up, then a Jew hearing the שם המפורש must surely stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the story of עגלון proves the judges must stand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עגלון had two reasons he 'should not' have needed to stand: he was a gentile, and he only heard a title, 'אלהים'. Even so, he stood. The judges are Jews and hear the real שם המפורש, so they must stand even more.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'how much more so' argument from a lighter case to a stronger one
A title or descriptive name of God, not His real Name

steps.whatToRemember: The judges stand when they hear the curse, learned by קל וחומר from עגלון, who stood even though he was a gentile who heard only a title of God.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that honoring God's Name is required even at the moment the Name is being repeated as part of a curse in court.

phrases.english: Isn't this a 'how much more so' argument?
If Eglon, king of Moab,
who was a gentile,
and knew (God) only by a title, stood up,
then a Jew, hearing the real Name,
how much more so (must he stand)!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the פסוק in step 16 proves the rule.
steps.raayaObject: The rule in the משנה that the judges stand when hearing the curse
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from עגלון, a gentile who stood on hearing only a title of God

steps.title: Where do we learn that the judges tear their clothes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the משנה's rule that the judges tear their clothes when they hear the blasphemy.
steps.simpleTranslation: The judges tear their clothes. Where do we learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next detail of the משנה, that the judges tear their garments, and asks for its source. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the previous steps the גמרא found a source for standing up. Now it asks the same kind of question about tearing. The question only asks for a source; it does not doubt the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we learn it?

phrases.english: They tear [their garments]: from where do we derive this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the source for standing, the גמרא turns to the next action in the משנה, tearing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A scriptural source showing that one who hears blasphemy must tear his clothes.

steps.title: The officials came to חזקיהו with torn clothes after hearing רבשקה
steps.stepSummary: The source is the פסוק in which אליקים, שבנא, and יואח came to חזקיהו with torn clothes after hearing רבשקה's blasphemy.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: "Then אליקים son of חלקיהו came, and so on, and שבנא the scribe and יואח son of אסף the recorder, to חזקיהו with torn garments, and they told him the words of רבשקה."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. It shows that חזקיהו's officials tore their clothes after hearing רבשקה insult God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבשקה, the Assyrian general, spoke against God. The officials who heard him came with torn garments. This shows that tearing is the proper reaction to hearing God's Name cursed.

keyTerms.meaning: The Assyrian officer who spoke against God outside ירושלים
And so on: the פסוק continues

phrases.english: As it is written: "Then came Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, etc.
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 18:37. The 'etc.' stands for the words the גמרא skips: 'who was over the household.'

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁבְנָא הַסֹּפֵר וְיוֹאָח בֶּן אָסָף הַמַּזְכִּיר
phrases.english: and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, son of Asaph, the recorder,
to Hezekiah with torn garments,
and they told him the words of Rabshakeh."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18 with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Those who heard רבשקה's blasphemy tore their garments (מלכים ב 18:37).

steps.title: Where do we learn that the tear is never sewn back?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the משנה's rule that the judges never fully sew the tear back together.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they do not sew it back together. Where do we learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next detail of the משנה, that the tear is not mended, and asks for its source. This sets up רבי אבהו's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about רבשקה showed that one must tear. It says nothing about whether the tear may be repaired. So a separate source is needed for this detail.

phrases.english: And they do not stitch [the tear back]: from where do we derive this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the obligation to tear to the follow-up rule that the tear may not be mended.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that a tear made for blasphemy may never be fully sewn back.

steps.title: רבי אבהו links the tearing for רבשקה to אלישע's tearing
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו makes a גזירה שוה from the word for tearing: the torn garments here, and אלישע tearing his garments when אליהו went up to heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: We learn it from the word "tearing" here and "tearing" there. Here it is written: "with torn garments." There it is written: "And אלישע saw it, and he cried: My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen. And he saw him no more, and he took hold of his clothes and tore them into two pieces."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers by connecting the two פסוקים that both use the word for tearing. Whatever we learn about אלישע's tear will also apply to the tear for blasphemy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a גזירה שוה: the same word in two places lets us carry a rule from one to the other. The פסוק about אלישע has an extra detail, "pieces," which the next step will explain. That detail then carries over to the tear made for רבשקה's blasphemy.

keyTerms.meaning: It is learned from the shared word "tearing" (a גזירה שוה)
It is written here… and it is written there
The prophet who was אליהו's student

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
It is derived from "tearing" [here] and "tearing" [there].
It is written here: "with torn garments,"
and it is written there: "And Elisha saw it, and he cried:
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 2:12, when אלישע watched אליהו go up to heaven.

phrases.english: My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen.
And he saw him no more, and he grabbed hold of his clothes
and tore them into two pieces."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: אָתְיָא קְרִיעָה קְרִיעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 by linking the פסוק from step 19 to the פסוק about אלישע.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה connects the tearing for רבשקה with אלישע's tearing, so the rule of אלישע's tear applies here too.

steps.title: The extra word "pieces" teaches the tear stays forever
steps.stepSummary: Since "tore them into two" already means pieces, the extra word "pieces" teaches that the garment stays torn forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: From the fact that it says "and tore them into two," don't I already know that they are pieces? So why does the פסוק say "pieces"? It teaches that they stay torn forever.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the word "pieces" seems extra in אלישע's פסוק and explains what it adds. Through the גזירה שוה from step 21, this proves that a tear for blasphemy may not be fully sewn back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once something is torn "into two," it is obviously in pieces, so the word "pieces" adds nothing new on its own. The extra word therefore teaches that the pieces must stay apart forever. The גזירה שוה carries this rule over to the tear made for blasphemy.

keyTerms.meaning: From the meaning of what is already said
Why does the פסוק need to say this? (pointing out an extra word)

steps.confusionAlert: "Torn forever" does not mean the garment can never be touched with a needle at all. It means it may not be sewn back so that it is fully whole again.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule that judges tear their clothes comes from the officials who heard רבשקה. The rule that the tear is never mended comes from the extra word "pieces" by אלישע, carried over through a גזירה שוה.

phrases.english: From the meaning of what is stated: "And tore them into two,"
do I not know that they are pieces?
So why does the verse say "pieces"?
It teaches that they remain torn forever.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the extra word in the פסוק that the גזירה שוה of step 21 relies on.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a tear for blasphemy may never be fully sewn back.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra word "קרעים" in מלכים ב 2:12, applied through the גזירה שוה.

steps.title: Both the direct hearer and the second-hand hearer must tear
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that both someone who hears the blasphemy himself and someone who hears it from that person must tear.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Both one who hears it himself and one who hears it from the one who heard it must tear his clothes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says who must tear. It includes even someone who hears the blasphemy second-hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think only someone who hears the actual מגדף has to tear. The ברייתא says hearing it repeated by someone else also requires tearing. This matches the officials in step 19, who tore after hearing רבשקה, and חזקיהו, who heard it from them.

keyTerms.meaning: One who hears from the mouth of a hearer, second-hand

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Both one who hears [the curse],
and one who hears it from the one who heard it,
is obligated to tear [his garments].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the sources for tearing, the גמרא clarifies who exactly must tear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both the direct hearer and the second-hand hearer of blasphemy must tear their garments.

steps.title: The witnesses do not tear again in court
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that the witnesses do not tear when they repeat the blasphemy in court, because they already tore when they first heard it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the witnesses do not have to tear, because they already tore at the time they heard it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with an exception for the witnesses who repeat the words in court. They do not tear a second time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hearing blasphemy normally requires tearing, but the witnesses already did so when they heard the מגדף himself. Saying the words again in court does not create a new obligation for them. The judges, who are hearing it for the first time, do tear.
steps.whatToRemember: Anyone who hears blasphemy, directly or second-hand, tears. The witnesses do not tear again in court, since they tore at the original hearing.

phrases.english: But the witnesses are not obligated to tear,
since they already tore at the time when they heard it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an exception to the general rule of step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses do not tear again when they testify, because they already tore when they first heard the blasphemy.

steps.title: Why don't the witnesses tear again when they hear it in court?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: tearing once in the past shouldn't exempt them, because right now in court they are hearing the blasphemy again.
steps.simpleTranslation: So what if they tore when they first heard it? They are hearing it again now!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא from Step 24, which said the witnesses don't tear in court because they already tore.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic of the challenge is that every hearing of the blasphemy should create a new obligation to tear. So the first tear should not cover the second hearing in court.

keyTerms.meaning: What of it? So what difference does that make?

phrases.english: And if they tore at the time that they heard it,
what of it?
But they are hearing it now!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי קָרְעוּ בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁשָּׁמְעוּ, מַאי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in Step 24
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's reason that the witnesses already tore when they first heard it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A new hearing should bring a new obligation, so an earlier tear should not exempt them now.

steps.title: Proof from King חזקיהו: only he tore, not the messengers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers from a פסוק: when the messengers reported רבשקה's words, חזקיהו tore his clothes, but the messengers did not tear again.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that. It says: 'When King חזקיהו heard the words of רבשקה, he tore his clothes.' The king tore, but they did not tear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a פסוק showing that people who repeat blasphemy they already heard do not tear a second time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק mentions only the king tearing when he heard the report. It says nothing about the messengers tearing again. From that the גמרא learns that someone repeating the blasphemy does not tear again, while a new listener does.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not enter your mind; don't think that
רבשקה, the Assyrian officer who blasphemed outside ירושלים

phrases.english: It should not enter your mind,
as it is written:
"And it was, when King Hezekiah heard
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 19:1

phrases.english: the words of Rabshakeh
that he tore his garments."
King Hezekiah tore,
but they did not tear.
phrases.notes: 'They' are the messengers who brought רבשקה's words to the king. They had already torn when they first heard it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 25
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every hearing requires a new tear, even for someone repeating it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Someone who repeats blasphemy he already heard and tore for does not tear again. Only the new listener tears.
steps.whatToRemember: The witnesses tear once, when they first hear. The judges tear when they hear it in court. The witnesses do not tear a second time, as we see from חזקיהו and his messengers.

steps.title: No tearing for blasphemy heard from a gentile
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל rules that one who hears blasphemy from a גוי does not have to tear.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: Someone who hears God's Name cursed by a גוי does not have to tear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling that limits the obligation to tear: it applies only when a Jew blasphemes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now we assumed that hearing blasphemy always requires tearing. שמואל adds a limit: it depends on who said it. This immediately raises a question about רבשקה, which the next step deals with.

keyTerms.meaning: Mention of God's Name (here, in a blasphemous way)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
One who hears a mention of God's Name from the mouth of a gentile
is not obligated to tear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new limit on the tearing obligation discussed so far
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blasphemy heard from a גוי does not require tearing.

steps.title: רבשקה was a Jew who left the faith
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא heads off a question from the חזקיהו story: they tore for רבשקה because he was a Jewish apostate, not a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will ask: what about רבשקה, whom they tore for? He was a Jew who had left the faith.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question against שמואל's rule from the story we just saw, and answers it in the same breath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The messengers and חזקיהו tore when they heard רבשקה, which seems to contradict שמואל's rule. The answer is that רבשקה was a ישראל מומר, so hearing blasphemy from him does require tearing.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say; introduces a question the speaker answers himself
A Jew who has abandoned Torah observance; an apostate

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read the question and the answer as two separate steps. The question about רבשקה is answered right away: he was Jewish, so tearing was required.

phrases.english: And if you will say: Rabshakeh —
phrases.notes: He means: they tore for רבשקה, so how can שמואל say we don't tear for a גוי?

phrases.english: he was an apostate Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends שמואל's rule from Step 27 against the רבשקה story in Step 26
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the blasphemer was Jewish
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבשקה was a גוי, yet they tore, which would contradict שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבשקה was a ישראל מומר, so tearing was required, and שמואל's rule stands.

steps.title: Tearing only for the unique Name of God
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל rules that one tears only for a curse using the שם המיוחד, not a substitute name.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה also said in the name of שמואל: We tear only for the special Name of God, not for a substitute name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second limit from שמואל: the kind of Name used in the blasphemy matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 limited tearing by who the speaker is. This step limits it by what Name was used. Only the שם המיוחד requires tearing; a כינוי does not.

keyTerms.meaning: The unique, special Name of God
A substitute name or title for God

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
One does not tear except
for the unique Name alone,
to exclude a substitute name, for which one does not tear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second limit on tearing from the same source as Step 27
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tearing applies only to blasphemy using the שם המיוחד, not a כינוי.

steps.title: רבי חייא: nowadays no tearing, which disagrees with שמואל on both points
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבי חייא disagrees with both of שמואל's rules. He holds that nowadays one does not tear, because otherwise the whole garment would be full of tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: These rulings disagree with רבי חייא on both points. רבי חייא said: Someone who hears God's Name cursed nowadays does not have to tear, because otherwise his whole garment would be filled with tears.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי חייא's ruling and points out that it argues with both of שמואל's rules from Steps 27 and 29.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא's only reason for not tearing nowadays is practical: blasphemy is so common that clothes would be shredded. That suggests he holds that by the basic law one would have to tear even in the cases שמואל exempts, such as a גוי or a כינוי. That is why the גמרא says he disagrees with שמואל on both points.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל: no tearing for a גוי and no tearing for a כינוי. רבי חייא: nowadays no tearing at all, only because it is too common, so he disagrees with שמואל on both.

phrases.english: And they disagree with Rabbi Chiya on both of them,
phrases.notes: "Both" means both of שמואל's rules: the one about a גוי and the one about a substitute name.

phrases.english: as Rabbi Chiya said:
One who hears a mention of God's Name nowadays
is not obligated to tear,
for if you do not say so,
the whole garment would be filled with tears.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets רבי חייא's view against both of שמואל's rules
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Nowadays one who hears blasphemy is exempt from tearing, because otherwise the garment would be full of tears.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows two different reasons for exempting someone from tearing: שמואל gives limits based on the speaker and the Name used, while רבי חייא gives a practical exemption for our times.

steps.title: Whose curses was רבי חייא talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose curses רבי חייא meant. A Jew would not curse so often, so it must be a גוי. A גוי does not know the שם המיוחד, so it must be a curse with a כינוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: From whom does one hear these curses? If you say from a Jew, are Jews so careless? Rather, obviously from a gentile. And if you say the special Name, do gentiles know it? Rather, it must be with a substitute name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of blasphemy רבי חייא had in mind when he said a garment would be full of tears. It answers its own question step by step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hearing blasphemy often enough to fill a garment with tears cannot come from Jews, because they are not that careless. So the speaker must be a גוי. A גוי does not know the שם המיוחד, so the curse must use a כינוי. Both of שמואל's exemptions turn out to be exactly the cases רבי חייא is talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a possibility the גמרא will reject)
A substitute name of ה׳, not the special Name

phrases.english: From whom?
phrases.notes: He means: from whom would a person hear the curses that רבי חייא said would fill his garment with tears?

phrases.english: If you say from a Jew,
are they so careless to such an extent?
Rather, it is obvious: from a gentile.
And if it means the special Name,
have they learned it?
phrases.notes: Gentiles don't know the special Name, so they couldn't curse with it.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not with a substitute name?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes רבי חייא's statement from Step 30 to pin down exactly which cases he meant.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of blasphemy (from whom, and with which name) רבי חייא meant when he said we don't tear nowadays.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Blasphemy from a גוי using a כינוי.

steps.title: Originally one did tear even for these curses
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי חייא only exempts these cases 'nowadays', it follows that originally one had to tear even for a גוי's curse with a כינוי. This goes against שמואל. The גמרא agrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: And learn from this: it is only nowadays that one does not tear, but originally one was obligated. Indeed, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from the last step and then confirms it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא said 'nowadays' we do not tear. That means the exemption is a later practical arrangement, not the basic law. So originally one had to tear for a גוי's curse and for a כינוי. This disagrees with both of שמואל's rules from Steps 27 and 29.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it / conclude from it

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי חייא, the basic law is that one tears even for a גוי's curse or a כינוי. Only nowadays do we not tear, because it happens too often. שמואל says there was never an obligation in those cases.

phrases.english: And learn from this:
it is only nowadays that one does not tear,
but originally, one was obligated.
Indeed, learn from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: בִּזְמַן הַזֶּה הוּא דְּלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the halachic result from the identification made in Step 31.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For רבי חייא, one originally had to tear even for a גוי's curse using a כינוי. Only nowadays is one exempt, against שמואל.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: 'I too, like him' is valid testimony
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה, where the second witness says only 'אף אני כמוהו'. ריש לקיש learns that such testimony is valid by Torah law, even in capital cases. Requiring each witness to say everything himself is only an extra standard set by the רבנן, and here they did not apply it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The second witness says: 'I too, like him.' ריש לקיש said: learn from this that 'I too, like him' is valid in monetary cases and in capital cases. Requiring more is a higher standard the רבנן made. Here, since it is not possible, the רבנן left it at Torah law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה about the second witness. ריש לקיש draws a general rule about witnesses from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally each witness gives his full testimony himself. In blasphemy, the curse should not be repeated, so the second witness only says 'אף אני כמוהו'. ריש לקיש explains that this short testimony is fully valid מדאורייתא. The usual requirement is only a מעלה (extra strictness) of the רבנן, and they dropped it here because it cannot be done.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I too, like him': a witness agreeing with the first witness's testimony

steps.confusionAlert: ריש לקיש is not saying the רבנן were lenient against the Torah. He is saying the Torah itself accepts this testimony. The רבנן simply did not add their usual extra requirement here.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a general rule about testimony: a witness agreeing with another witness's words is valid by Torah law. It matters well beyond blasphemy cases.

phrases.english: The second witness says:
"I too, like him."
Reish Lakish said:
Learn from this,
that "I too, like him" is valid
in monetary cases and in capital cases,
and it is a higher standard that the Rabbis made.
phrases.notes: The higher standard is that each witness must say his whole testimony himself.

phrases.english: And here, since it is not possible,
the Rabbis left it on Torah law.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשֵּׁנִי אוֹמֵר: ״אַף אֲנִי כָּמוֹהוּ״. אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of tearing and returns to a new line of the משנה about the second witness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'אף אני כמוהו' is valid testimony by Torah law in both monetary and capital cases. The requirement for full separate testimony is only a rabbinic מעלה.

steps.title: Proof: we would never execute on invalid testimony
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש proves his point. If 'אף אני כמוהו' were invalid by Torah law, we could not execute the blasphemer just because full testimony is impossible here.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you thought it is invalid, would we execute a man here just because it is not possible?
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש backs up his rule from the last step with a logical proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה does execute the blasphemer based on the second witness saying only 'אף אני כמוהו'. Being unable to do something is no reason to kill a person on testimony that is invalid. So this testimony must be valid by Torah law.

keyTerms.meaning: If it entered your mind (if you thought)

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש's logic: since the משנה executes based on 'אף אני כמוהו', it must be valid by Torah law. The usual demand for full separate testimony is only a rabbinic extra.

phrases.english: For if you thought it is invalid,
here, because it is not possible,
would we execute the man?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports ריש לקיש's rule in Step 33 with a reductio argument.
steps.raayaObject: That 'אף אני כמוהו' is valid by Torah law.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה executes the blasphemer on such testimony. We would never execute on invalid testimony just because full testimony is impossible.

steps.title: The anonymous משנה follows רבי עקיבא about a third witness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line that the third witness also says 'אף אני כמוהו'. It explains that this unnamed משנה follows רבי עקיבא, who compares three witnesses to two.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And the third witness says: I too heard like him.' The unnamed author of the משנה holds like רבי עקיבא, who compares three witnesses to two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another line from the משנה, that even a third witness must say 'אף אני כמוהו'. It tells us which תנא this anonymous משנה follows: רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two witnesses are already enough, so why does the משנה make a third witness speak at all? Because רבי עקיבא holds that three witnesses are judged exactly like two, so the third is a full part of the testimony group. That is why the משנה requires him to testify as well.

keyTerms.meaning: An unnamed, anonymous statement in a משנה (a סְתָם מִשְׁנָה) with no תנא's name attached
The third one, meaning the third witness
Compares, treats one case exactly like another (from הֶקֵּשׁ)
Three to two, meaning three witnesses are treated just like two witnesses

steps.whatToRemember: The anonymous משנה follows רבי עקיבא: a third witness counts fully like the first two, so he too must testify ('אף אני כמוהו').
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the third witness is needed to make the testimony work, because two witnesses are enough. The point is that once he is there, רבי עקיבא counts him as a full member of the testimony.

phrases.english: And the third says:
"I too [heard] like him."
The unnamed [משנה] is like Rabbi Akiva,
who compares three to two.
phrases.notes: This comparison comes from the פסוק that speaks of 'two witnesses or three witnesses' (דברים 17:6).

steps.triggerLanguage: סְתָמָא כְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, דְּמַקֵּישׁ שְׁלֹשָׁה לִשְׁנַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After discussing whether 'אף אני כמוהו' is valid testimony (Steps 33-34), the גמרא now looks at a further detail of the משנה: why a third witness must speak too.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The anonymous משנה requiring the third witness to say 'אף אני כמוהו' follows רבי עקיבא, who treats three witnesses as equal to two.
